newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed starts new peace talks with Chechen rebels.
newsitem.headline: Lebed starts new peace talks with Chechen rebels.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed arrived in Chechnya for talks with rebel leaders on Thursday, promising to discuss prisoner exchanges and compliance with a ceasefire agreed last month.

The political status of the breakaway region would not be on the agenda, Interfax news agency quoted Lebed as saying en route to the village of Novye Atagi, some 25 km (15 miles) south of the Chechen capital Grozny.

His talks there with separatist chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov take place less than a week after the two signed an ambitious peace deal in the region. The deal postpones any decision about Chechnya's political status for five years.

The rebels, who celebrate the fifth anniversary of their unilateral declaration of independence on Friday, view Chechnya as a separate state, while Moscow says the oil-rich region must stay part of the vast Russian Federation.
Lebed admitted that the peace deal was not final yet.
"Peace in Chechnya has many enemies, many hotheads and empty heads whose actions can derail the peace process," he said.
Interfax quoted Lebed as telling reporters he was worried by reports about separatists seizing hostages and persecuting supporters of pro-Moscow authorities in the breakaway region.
Rebel leaders have denied the reports.

Lebed is President Boris Yeltsin's representative in Chechnya. But the 65-year-old president, on holiday near Moscow, has not publicly backed Lebed's peace deal. Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has given the accord his guarded approval.

One key question is the shape of a future Chechen administration. Lebed, quoted by Itar-Tass news agency, said he favoured a coalition government comprising separatist leaders, members of the Moscow-backed Chechen administration and members of the Chechen diaspora.

Doku Zavgayev, head of the Moscow-backed administration, told Ekho Moskvy radio he was ready to broaden his government to include "Dudayevists" -- separatists loyal to former rebel leader Dzhokhar Dudayev.
Dudayev was killed in a rocket attack in April but the wild Chechen rumour mill says he could return to Grozny to mark independence day.
One rebel reportedly killed in another Russian raid, rebel commander Salman Raduyev, has already returned, and he insisted that Dudayev was still alive.
Interfax said Maskhadov had promised to ban independence day parades in Grozny in favour of religious ceremonies.
The separatists who control Grozny have already started administering strict Islamic law as punishment for drunkenness and other crimes.
Much of the city is in ruins and it will take a long time for things to return to normal. Tens of thousands of people have been killed in 21 months of fighting.

Fery Aalame, head of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Grozny, said on Wednesday some 80,000 to 100,000 people may have been forced to flee Grozny in the latest fighting, which started when the rebels caputured Grozny on August 6 and the Russian military then threatened to destroy the town.
"The civilian population has suffered a lot, there is a complete lack of clean water...there is no medical structure," Aalame told reporters in Grozny on Wednesday.
The Red Cross is helping to restart water supplies and was bringing in some 600,000 litres (132,000 gallons) a day to the civilian population. It is also supplying food and medicines.
